rewritten_text:
The first chance I got to catch Tom by himself I asked him what his notion had been, back at the evasion—what he meant to do supposing it all come off right and he succeeded in freeing a nigger that was free already? And he said the thing he'd had in his mind right from the beginning, provided we fetched Jim out safe, was to take him downriver on the raft, and keep having adventures clean to the river's mouth, and then let him know he was free, and carry him home again on a steamboat, grand style, and pay for all his time, and send word on ahead to gather all the niggers round about, and let them march him into town by torchlight with a brass-band, and that would make a hero of him, and us too. But I judged things had turned out about as well as they could.

We got Jim clear of his chains mighty quick, and when Aunt Polly and Uncle Silas and Aunt Sally heard how well he'd helped the doctor tend Tom, they made a powerful fuss over him, and fitted him out first-rate, and let him eat everything he wanted, and enjoy himself with no work to do. We fetched him into the sick-room, too, and had a grand talk; and Tom handed Jim forty dollars for putting up with being our prisoner so patient and carrying it off so fine, and Jim was almost beside himself with pleasure, and broke out saying:

“_Dah_, Huck, now, what did I tell you?—what I say to you back dah on Jackson islan'? I _tole_ you 'bout my hairy breas', en de sign dat goes wid it; en I _tole_ you I'd been rich one time, en was gwyne be rich _agin_; en now it's true; en heah de money _is! Dah_, now! doan' you argue wid _me_—signs means _signs_, you min' me; en I knowed I'd be rich agin jis' as sure as I knows I'm standin' heah dis very minute!”

Then Tom kept on talking and talking, and says, le's us three slip away some night and get us an outfit, and go have roaring adventures among the Injuns out in the Territory, for a couple weeks or so; and I says, all right, that agrees with me, only I ain't got money to buy an outfit, and I don't reckon I could fetch any from home, because pap's likely come back by now and took it all off Judge Thatcher and drunk the whole of it.

“No, he ain't,” says Tom; “it's every bit there still—over six thousand dollars; and your pap hasn't been back at all since.

Smallpox!

I leaped to the king and spoke into his ear:

“Through the door at once, sire! This woman is dying of the sickness that laid waste the outskirts of Camelot two years since.”

He never stirred.

“Indeed I mean to stay—and to give help as well.”

Once more I whispered:

“King, you cannot do this. You must leave.”

“Your purpose is kind, and your words are wise enough. Yet it would shame a king to show fear, and shame a belted knight to refuse his aid when there are those in need of succor. Be still; I shall not leave. You must be the one to go. The ban of the Church rests not upon me, but you are forbidden here, and heavily will she punish you if knowledge of your trespass reach her.”

His situation was perilous, and could well cost his life, but arguing would accomplish nothing. Once he thought his honor as a knight concerned in the matter, discussion was finished; he would remain, and nothing could move him; that I knew. So I let the matter rest. The woman said:

“Good sir, will ye kindly mount that ladder and tell me what ye discover? Fear not to speak the truth, for a time may come when a mother's heart itself can break no further—having broken already.”

“Stay,” the king said, “and feed the woman. I shall go.” He laid the knapsack down.

I turned to go, but the king was before me. He stopped, looking down at a man stretched in the faint light, who till then had neither spoken nor taken notice of us.

“Is this your husband?” asked the king.

“Yes.”

“Does he sleep?”

“God be praised for that single mercy, yes—for three hours now. How shall I ever discharge the debt of my thankfulness! My heart is full to bursting with gratitude for the sleep that is upon him.”

I said:

“We shall take care. We won't disturb him.”

“Ah, no, ye will not do that, for he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes, and what a victory to be certain of it! No one can hurt him now, no one offer him another insult. He is happy now in heaven; or, should he not be there, he rests content in hell; for neither abbot nor bishop will he encounter in that place. We were children together, boy and girl; for five and twenty years we have been husband and wife, never parted until today. Consider what a long while that is for loving and suffering side by side. This morning his wits were wandering, and he imagined us boy and girl once more, roaming the joyful fields; and with that happy, innocent talk he roamed farther and farther, chatting lightly still, till he passed into those other fields unknown to us, and vanished from the sight of living men.

The elegant gentlemen of the best families wore small dangling ornaments that jingled as they moved lazily about. These golden chains rang like costly little bells. Between their ringing and the rustle of silk, patterned fabric, and fine linen, the air seemed to stir enough to blow Saint Antoine and his terrible hunger far away.

Fine clothes were the one reliable magic charm for keeping everything in its proper place. Everyone was dressed for a costume ball that would never end. The ball stretched from the Palace of the Tuileries through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the legislative chambers, the courts of justice, and all of society except its ragged scarecrows, right down to the public executioner. To keep the spell working, even he had to perform his duties with curled and powdered hair, a coat trimmed with gold, light shoes, and white silk stockings. He presided over the gallows and the breaking wheel—the axe was seldom used—in this delicate outfit. His fellow executioners in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans and the others, called him Monsieur Paris, following the bishops' fashion of using place names. And who at Monseigneur's reception in the year 1780 could possibly doubt that a system resting on a hangman in curls, powder, gold trim, dainty shoes, and white silk stockings would outlast the stars themselves!

After relieving his four servants of their duties and drinking his chocolate, Monseigneur had the doors of his innermost holy room opened and stepped out. What submission followed, what crawling, flattery, and servile self-abasement! His worshippers bowed so low in both body and soul that they had none of that devotion left for Heaven—which may have been one reason, among others, why they never bothered it.

Offering a promise here, a smile there, a whisper to one fortunate slave and a wave to another, Monseigneur graciously made his way through his rooms to the distant outer boundary of Truth. There he turned around and made the journey back. In time, the little spirits who served his chocolate shut him inside his sanctuary again, and he disappeared from view.

With the performance finished, the fluttering air rose into a small storm, and the expensive little bells rang their way downstairs. Soon just one man remained from the whole crowd. Holding his hat under his arm and his snuffbox in his hand, he walked slowly past the mirrors toward the exit.

“I give you over,” this man said, pausing at the last doorway and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

Then he shook the snuff off his fingers as though shaking the dust from his feet, and walked quietly down the stairs.
